title: When They Call You a Terrorist: A Black Lives Matter Memoir
author: Patrisse Khan-Cullors
asha bandele
target_audience: Readers interested in the Black Lives Matter movement
Those seeking insight into contemporary racial and social justice issues
Students and educators in African American studies, sociology, and history
General readers of memoirs and social commentary
core_themes: Racial injustice and systemic racism in the United States
The personal and societal impact of mass incarceration and police violence
Family, resilience, and community in the face of adversity
The genesis and goals of the Black Lives Matter movement
primary_purpose: To provide a personal account of Patrisse Khan-Cullors' life, the events and influences that led her to co-found the Black Lives Matter movement, and to highlight the significance and human cost of systemic racism, while also uplifting narratives of resilience, love, and collective activism.

structure_format.narrative_style: Personal, reflective, and poetic; storytelling blended with social commentary; first-person perspective
structure_format.organization: Chronological, interweaving Khan-Cullors' personal story with key moments in the Black Lives Matter movement and larger racial justice struggles
features: Historical and contemporary context of racial injustice
Exploration of intersections between personal trauma and political activism
Afterword and resources for further learning

key_concepts_lessons: Systemic racism is deeply embedded in American institutions and lives.
Personal experience can spark collective action and movement building.
Black Lives Matter emerged in response to unchecked police violence and criminalization of Black communities.
Activism is deeply rooted in love for self, family, and community.
The narratives about terrorism and criminality are often wielded to delegitimize Black protest and activists.
Healing, self-care, and solidarity are essential components of sustained social justice work.
notable_features: Firsthand account from a co-founder of Black Lives Matter
Blends memoir with political analysis and movement history
Highlights intersectionality and personal/familial impacts of activism
Accessible for a general audience but informed by deep scholarship and lived experience
cultural_historical_context: Published in the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement’s rapid growth, following the killings of Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown, and others. The book situates Khan-Cullors’ life and activism within the ongoing struggle against anti-Black racism, mass incarceration, and state violence in America, drawing from both the Ferguson era and earlier civil rights battles as context.
reception_impact: Bestseller and critically acclaimed for its powerful writing and insight
Praised by activists, scholars, and reviewers for its emotional resonance and depth
Nominated for several book awards, including NAACP Image Awards
Used widely in educational and activist settings to foster discussion on race and justice
Helped further mainstream understanding of the Black Lives Matter movement and its aims
comparable_titles: The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin
Between the World and Me by Ta-Nehisi Coates
Men We Reaped by Jesmyn Ward
